processing: Traditionally handmade through natural drying, special pressing and packing, with heavy, repeated post-fermentation that turns the colour red-brown.
harvest_season: Mature leaf and red stem rather than a prized early picking; coarse grades dominate what Tibetan regions drink.
appearance_dry: Dark brown compressed tea, stalkier in the coarse grades.
appearance_wet: Dark brown leaf, often with stem.
taste_profile: Mellow and long-lasting; a sturdy base for butter and salt.

brewing.notes: Simmer broken pieces for the traditional cup, or brew 7 g in 150 ml with short steeps to taste it plain.

vintage_note: Sold in pressed forms under product names such as kang zhuan and jin jian, with year and maker on the pack rather than a harvest season. Dark tea of this kind stores well, so both recent and older stock exist. Quality varies widely, so choose a maker you can identify.
description:
Nan Lu Bian Cha, South Road border tea, is the dark tea of Ya'an in Sichuan, also called Ya'an border tea or simply Tibetan tea. It is the historic supply for Tibet, Qinghai and the Tibetan areas of Ganzi and Aba.

The method is built around repeated post-fermentation and pressing. The trade separated finer teas such as mao jian from the coarser jin yu, jin cang and kang zhuan, and it is the coarser teas that Tibetan drinkers mostly use.

The cup is bright red-brown and mellow, and it lasts well. Drunk plain it is calm and woody; churned with butter and salt, or with walnut as some recipes have it, it becomes something else entirely.

Buy by product name and maker. Heavy price competition in this market has hurt quality, so a cheap brick with no clear producer is a poor bet.
history:
Tea from the Ya'an area was moving towards Tibet by the Tang and Song periods, and this route became bound up with the tea-horse trade. Six Song-era tea-horse offices are recorded within today's Ya'an, with Yazhou, Yingjing, Diaomen and Lizhou the best known.

Successive governments treated Sichuan border tea as official tea for the plateau. Today its making is listed as Chinese national intangible heritage under dark tea craft, and the listing itself notes falling standards in the market.
